And the change was that their product market fit disappeared. Now it's not that their product all of a sudden become irrelevant, people simply wanted something else. (00:14:48): So when product market fit disappeared, you actually need to go back to square one. And the faster that you realize and you basically say everything that I know so far, everything that I knew so far is irrelevant anymore. Can I restart? Can I go back to square one and restart? Because if you cannot, you will die. You're following your own solution and you believe that this solution is going to be marketed better than what the market wants. And what the market wants is different. (00:15:25): It can be also a matter of regulation change. One of my startups called Fibo died because of change in regulation. So Fibo was doing tax returns, something that everyone hates, but we have to do that. And when we started we basically say wait a minute, when I speak with people and ask them how is tax returns being done in your country, what I heard was pretty consistent, it's either complex or expensive or both, that's it. And I said wait a minute, what if I can simplify that? What if we can make it really, really simple? (00:16:08): And we define simplification by filing in less than five minutes. Whatever you do, if you can do that in less than five minutes, it's simple enough. And we ended up with building a platform in Israel that people were able to file in less than three minutes. And that was actually pretty amazing. Now the result was that in about ... In Israel filing is not mandatory. So we actually enable people that were not filing up until now to file because it's simple. And we increased the size of the market by 25% over one year.
turns.zh:
总的来说，我想说的是，当一天结束时，我们审视全球危机时会说：“哦，这会影响某个行业。”但作为创业者，你不关心整个行业，只关心自己的初创公司，仅此而已。如果全球其他地方也遭遇同样的问题，对你毫无帮助，半点用处都没有。所以你的问题就是你的问题，仅此而已。（00:10:39）然后你需要抽象化这一点，基本意识到，等等，我要把危机定义为你原本拥有但后来消失的重要事物。比如说，你原本有数百万美元的收入，但突然最大的客户决定不再合作，你失去了一半收入。突然间你会说：“等等，我必须适应，发生了重大变化。”（00:11:10）而这个重大变化可能是收入消失、资金链断裂、市场预测失准，或者失去大客户等等。总之，第一类危机围绕现金展开。突然间你的现金流与预期不符，可能是因为资金链断裂、收入下滑、市场预测失准，或者失去大客户。这时你需要调整策略。（00:11:43）第二类危机更为严重，那就是产品市场失配。这可能由监管政策、竞争环境、突发事件导致产品价值消失。我们回归本质，产品市场匹配很简单——即为客户创造价值。历史上没有不解决产品市场匹配问题的公司，它们最终都会消亡。（00:12:20）顺便说一下，产品市场匹配通常只有一个衡量标准——用户留存率。只要你创造了价值，用户就会回来，仅此而已。如果用户不回来，说明你没有创造价值。在创业初期，这将是首个阶段，需要大量迭代和失败尝试。我们尝试某种方法，如果不成功，就换一种，直到找到有效方案。（00:12:54）但一旦你找到了方向，就可以进入下一阶段。但如果一切都崩塌了呢？如果监管政策突然改变？依赖的独特数据被他人获取？竞争对手让你的产品过时了？（00:13:22）我用iPhone很久了，显然很多人也用iPhone。2007年iPhone问世之前，我们用带按键的手机。iPhone推出时，微软断言它注定失败。作为市场领导者，微软拥有运行于全球几乎所有手机的Windows移动操作系统，从诺基亚、摩托罗拉到三星，无所不包。他们认为iPhone永远行不通，完全没意识到其影响力。于是一个完全不同的产品进入市场，不仅颠覆行业，还给其他所有人带来危机。（00:14:15）结果如今微软已退出移动操作系统市场，诺基亚也消失了
许多公司消失了，摩托罗拉也倒闭了，几乎所有在这个行业中举足轻重的公司，都未能及时适应变革。而变革的核心在于，他们的产品市场定位不再适用了。现在，倒不是说他们的产品突然变得无关紧要了，只是人们想要其他东西了。（00:14:48）所以当产品市场定位消失时，你实际上需要从头再来。你越快意识到这一点，就越需要说出“到目前为止我所知道的一切，都已经过时了”。我能重新开始吗？我能回到原点，重新开始吗？因为如果做不到，你就会死掉。你固守自己的解决方案，坚信它能比市场需求更胜一筹。但市场需求早已变了。（00:15:25）这也可能是监管政策的变化导致的。我的初创公司Fibo就因为监管政策的变动而倒闭了。Fibo当时做的是税务申报——这是一项人人都厌恶但又不得不做的事情。我们刚开始时想，等等，跟别人聊聊你们国家的税务申报流程，得到的反馈基本一致：要么流程复杂，要么费用高昂，要么两者兼有。我说，等等，如果我能把它简化呢？如果能让它变得极其简单呢？（00:16:08）我们的简化标准是申报时间不超过五分钟。只要能在五分钟内完成操作，就算足够简单了。最终我们在以色列开发了一个平台，用户只需三分钟就能完成申报。这成果相当惊人。不过以色列的申报并非强制性。所以我们让那些此前从不申报的人也开始申报，因为操作简单。一年内，我们的市场规模就增长了25%。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Of people filing taxes?
turns.zh: 关于报税的人呢？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Yep. Because it was simple. So you go into the platform, you realize that wait a minute, I actually entitled to get a return, so let me file. If I'm not entitled to get a return, then I'm not going to file because it's not mandatory. And the result is that we increased the load of the taxation system. And all of a sudden the Israeli tax authority didn't like us anymore and they basically shut us down. So changing the regulation and we lost product market fit overnight. They basically say, "Oh, we are going to shut you down and that's tomorrow." And that's it. (00:17:22): Now we did not have enough run rate to actually ... because the company was about break even, so we did not have enough funding to go and try to find something else. And we tried to fight the regulator, but fighting regulator requires a long period of time and a lot of funding and we did not have that. (00:17:49): So regulation might be a reason why you lose product market fit. And you need to go back to square one. And what we decided is that, okay, what I decided on a personal level is that I'm not going deal with the regulation anymore. I don't want to rely on a regulator to allow me or not allow me to do what I want to do. (00:18:16): By the way, with Waze, in the early days we thought that the business model is going to be selling data to authorities, to municipalities, to maybe public transportation systems and so forth. And we basically say wait a minute, we have the best traffic information in the world, I can go to a municipality and tell them how long does it take to make a left turn in each and every traffic light in the city every day of the week, every hour of the day. And therefore they can recalibrate the traffic control system and enable better utilization of the entire road system. And it turns out that this is really, really, really slow business development process. They didn't really care. And that was frustrating. Even if you offer that for free they still don't care. And the result is that we changed the business model and we ended up with advertisement. But the reality is that I don't like to work with regulators, that is all.
turns.zh: 是的。因为这很简单。所以你进入平台后，会意识到，等等，我实际上有权获得退税，那我就去申请退税。如果我没有资格获得退税，那我就不会去申请，因为这不是强制性的。结果，我们增加了税务系统的负担。突然之间，以色列税务局不喜欢我们了，他们基本上把我们关停了。所以调整法规导致我们一夜之间失去了产品市场适应性。他们基本上说，“哦，我们要关停你们，就在明天。”然后就这样了。（00:17:22）：现在我们没有足够的运营速度来真正……因为公司快要达到收支平衡了，所以我们没有足够的资金去寻找其他机会。我们试图与监管机构抗争，但与监管机构抗争需要很长时间和大量资金，而我们没有这些。（00:17:49）：所以监管问题可能是你失去产品市场适应性的一个原因。你需要从头再来。而我们决定的是，好吧，我个人决定不再与监管机构打交道。我不想依赖监管机构来允许我或不允许我做我想做的事。（00:18:16）：顺便说一句，Waze早期我们认为商业模式将是向当局、市政当局、公共交通系统等出售数据。我们基本上说，等等，我们有世界上最好的交通信息，我可以去市政当局告诉他们，一周每一天，每个小时，在城市每个红绿灯左转需要多长时间。因此，他们可以重新校准交通控制系统，更好地利用整个道路系统。结果发现，这是一个非常、非常、非常缓慢的业务发展过程。他们并不真正在乎。即使你免费提供，他们也不在乎。结果我们改变了商业模式，最终转向了广告。但现实是，我不喜欢与监管机构合作，仅此而已。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. There's so much here I want to dig into. One is this example, this story about losing product market fit, it reminds me of, I had Drew Houston on the podcast, the founder of Dropbox, and he described a moment where when Apple launched Apple Photos or iCloud, I think it was iCloud, he's like, "It's as if there's this mushroom cloud exploding far in the distance that you don't hear for a long time and we didn't necessarily see exactly how much this will have impacted our business." And I think that's what happens a lot of cases. You see something happen and you're like, "No, this is no problem, we're going to win anyway." Like Blackberry I think did the same thing with iPhone.
turns.zh: 好的。这里有很多我想深入探讨的地方。一个是这个例子，关于失去产品市场适应性的故事，这让我想起，我在播客上采访过Dropbox的创始人德鲁·休斯顿，他描述了苹果推出Apple Photos或iCloud（我认为是iCloud）的时候，他说：“就好像远处有朵蘑菇云在爆炸，你很久都听不到声音，我们也不一定能准确看到这会对我们的业务产生多大影响。” 我认为很多情况下都是这样的。你看到一些事情发生，然后你会说，“不，这不是问题，我们无论如何都会赢的。” 比如黑莓在面对iPhone时就做出了同样的选择。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: We had the same thing with Waze, because when we started Waze was free and it was the only one that was offering turn-by-turn navigation free. And the reason is that we created our own maps. And then one day in 2010, Google announced their free turn-by-turn navigation. Turns out that they were working for the last two years in building maps of the US. And they enabled that on Google Maps, turn-by-turn navigation with audio guidance to turn right, turn left and so forth. (00:20:38): And two companies were actually shocked, the entire industry, but two companies were impacted. The first one is actually TomTom. TomTom was the provider of the maps for Google to do navigation. And they basically say, "No, we have our own maps, we are going to terminate the contract." And TomTom said, "Wait a minute, you are paying us $18 million a year and we have five years contract." And Google say, "Yeah, we will keep on paying you that amount of money that we are committed, but we are not going to use your product anymore." (00:21:11): And that one was Waze because basically everyone in the industry told us that we are doomed. Our own investors told us that, "Look, if we can sell the company for $20 or $30 million today, do it because you are not going to be successful." (00:21:27): Now obviously we turned the corner and turned out to be very successful. And to that level that eventually Google acquired us. And the reason is that the use case was different. Waze was focusing on the daily commuters. So we wanted people to use our application twice a day, when you go to the office and when you come back home. And Google Maps is something that you are being used not that frequent, you are in general I would say if I ask a hundred people how often they use Waze, they will tell me every day. If I ask them how often they use Google Maps, they will tell me, "When I need it." So a different use case and obviously different product that is built for the specificity of the use case. So Waze is way simpler and the map looks almost abstractive, they're not, but looks like abstractive and way less details. And the result is the ability to create something that is simpler and people are using every day. (00:22:34): But when Google announced turn-by-turn navigation, all the investors in the world turn their back on us. And that was 2010. We were looking for new funding. I remember that night, because we were just about to go and meet with all partners meeting at Khosla Ventures. And we had multiple meetings beforehand and that was like, okay, this is the final seal. (00:23:07): And the evening before we had dinner with the partners that was promoting us at Khosla Ventures and he told us, "Look, I have a lot of relationship in the industry, and I spoke with my friends at Google and they told me that they are at least two years away from building their own maps." And the next morning they simply announced this turn-by-turn navigation. Going to that meeting was a waste of time already. And we had very, very hard time to raise capital because of that. (00:23:38): But eventually we were lucky in the sense that once Google announced their turn-by-turn navigation, turns out that the rest of the industry were took by surprise. And Microsoft decided that wait a minute, we don't have our own maps, so let's invest in Waze. So we ended up getting investment from someone that we did not expect.
turns.zh:
我们在Waze上也遇到过类似的情况。当时Waze刚推出时是免费的，而且是唯一提供免费实时导航服务的应用。原因在于我们自主开发了地图。2010年的一天，谷歌宣布推出免费实时导航功能。原来他们过去两年一直在构建美国地图数据库，并在Google Maps上推出了带有语音提示的实时导航功能，比如"右转"、"左转"等指示。（00:20:38）  
两家公司因此震惊了整个行业，但其中两家受到了巨大冲击。第一家是TomTom。TomTom曾为谷歌提供导航地图，但双方合同即将到期时，谷歌突然终止合作，称"我们将继续按合同支付费用，但不再使用你们的产品"。（00:21:11）  
Waze当时也面临巨大压力。业内普遍认为我们注定失败，投资者甚至建议"以2000万至3000万美元出售公司"。（00:21:27）  
但最终我们成功扭转局面，谷歌甚至收购了我们。关键在于用例差异：Waze专注于日常通勤用户，用户每天使用两次；Google Maps则用得较少。（00:22:34）  
2010年谷歌宣布实时导航时，所有投资者都转身离去。我们当时正寻求新融资。记得那晚，我们即将在Khosla Ventures与合作伙伴会面，此前已多次沟通，原以为万事俱备。（00:23:07）  
但前晚与Khosla Ventures的推荐伙伴共进晚餐时，他透露"谷歌至少还需两年时间才能完成地图构建"。次日清晨，谷歌却突然发布实时导航功能。这次会面成了徒劳之举，融资之路异常艰难。（00:23:38）  
不过谷歌最终推出实时导航后，整个行业都措手不及。微软随即决定投资Waze，扭转了局面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So first of all, you've shared all these types of crisis, I think it might be helpful to do a quick taxonomy of the types of crisis founders face. You shared regulation changes, competitors coming at you, investors not wanting to invest.
turns.zh: 好的。首先，你提到了各种类型的危机，我觉得对创始人面临的危机类型做一个快速分类可能会有帮助。你提到了监管政策的变化、竞争对手的挑战、投资者不愿投资等情况。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: So two types of, abstractly, two types of crisis. One is that I would call that a cash crisis. So all of a sudden your cash program or plan is being jeopardized, for losing a customer, disappearing investor, not meeting your expectation, dramatic price change in the market and so forth. And the other one is lose of product market fit. So all of a sudden whatever you have is irrelevant anymore and you actually need to go back to square one. (00:24:54): For the first type of crisis, if this is a cash crisis, then what you really need to ask yourself, and in any type crisis, first of all is what is actually being impacted? Is that my run rate, is that my product, is that my revenue stream? If I'm still relevant? (00:25:19): With Order.chat, we were irrelevant, that's it. And so the first thing that you need to do is what is really being impacted? And then the second thing is how long it's going to last? Is that a temporary thing? Is that forever? Is that the new future? And then you ask yourself, okay, so how much run rate do I have? And you re-plan accordingly. (00:25:52): And I'll give you some examples, and this is really important, because let's say that you're a company that we have $5 million of revenues a year, say 400,000 per month, and your burn rate, your net burn rate is 200,000. So you actually at the end of the year, in order to run for a year, you need about two and a half million dollars to run. If you lose half of the revenues, and you only had two and a half million in the bank, you now have six month to run. So obviously you need to re-adapt. (00:26:36): Now, one of the things that you might say to yourself, "I'm going to remain on the same course and I'm going to deal with the crisis in five month from now." Or you can basically say, "No, I'm going to change my expense to adjust to the current revenue stream that I have and still have 12 month of run rate." (00:26:58): Whatever you are going to decide, you are going to decide, you need to decide today, right now. And the reason is very simple, if you want to reduce the burn, the expenses in order to extend the run rate, if you wait two more month, then it's going to become nearly impossible to do. If you wait six more month, then obviously this is impossible to do. So the longer that you wait, you actually lose options. The only ability to choose is today. This is one of the most challenging part of a crisis. You actually need to make a decision rapidly, like today. (00:27:41): There are few reasons to that. Number one is that if you don't then you might lose options. Number two, and this is about communicating within the organization that decision. Look, if there is a crisis everyone knows, everyone knows, and you don't do anything about it, this is not a good practice. Now you might want to decide, no, we're going to keep on running full steam ahead until we hit the wall because by that we increase the likelihood that we will have enough velocity to bypass the wall. But you need to communicate that with your team because the one that is really suffer is not just you, it's the entire team. They know that there is a crisis and they want to know that someone that holds the steering wheel is making the decisions. And if you don't, then guess what? You are then a sinking ship. And what's going to happen is that the top performing people, they would leave.
turns.zh:
简单来说，危机可以分为两种类型。第一种是资金危机。例如，突然间你的现金计划受到威胁——客户流失、投资者撤资、收入低于预期、市场价格剧烈波动等等。而第二种危机是产品市场适配性丧失。这意味着你的产品或服务突然变得过时，需要从头再来。

（00:24:54）对于资金危机，你首先需要自问：真正受影响的是什么？是收入增长率？是产品质量？还是收入来源？你是否仍具竞争力？（00:25:19）以Order.chat为例，我们当时的处境就是产品与市场脱节。首先要确认核心影响因素，然后判断危机持续时间：是暂时波动？还是永久性变革？接着重新规划资源配置。

（00:25:52）举个例子：假设一家公司年收入500万美元，月均40万美元，净亏损20万美元。若收入减半，仅剩250万美元现金储备，公司最多可维持两个半月运营。此时你需要迅速调整策略：是坚持原计划等待五个月后再调整，还是立即优化成本以维持12个月的运营周期？

（00:26:58）无论何种选择，都必须当下决断。若想延长运营周期需减少开支，若再等两个月几乎不可能实现，若再等六个月则彻底无望。时间拖延意味着选择权丧失，决策必须即刻做出。

（00:27:41）关键在于两点：第一，避免错失良机；第二，及时向团队传达决策。若危机发生却无所作为，必将酿成大祸。有些公司选择“撞墙前全速前进”，试图通过增加速度突破困境，但必须与团队沟通——受影响的不只是你，还有整个团队。他们需要确信有人掌舵决策，否则公司将陷入困境，优秀人才必将离职。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me do a quick summary of what you've shared to give people a landscape and then let's keep going down this route. So there's basically two types of crisis. And there's small crisis, I imagine someone's pissed off at something. These are how you describe major crisis, like existential crisis for your startup. Is that the way to think about it?
turns.zh: 让我快速总结一下你分享的内容，让大家有个整体了解，然后我们再继续探讨。基本上，危机分为两种类型。小型危机，比如有人因为某件事生气了。而大危机，比如初创企业的生存危机。你们是这么看的吗？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Right. Because if an A-player leaves, I hate it, but it's not a crisis.
turns.zh: 对。毕竟如果一个A级员工离职了，虽然我会很不开心，但这还不算危机。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Okay, cool. So there's two, cash crisis, which is either a bunch of revenue disappears or investors bail or don't want to keep supporting you. Those are the two major buckets. And then there's product market fit crisis, could be a competitor launches, could be the market changes, things like that. (00:29:28): And within the cash crisis, so say you realize we don't have as much cash as we planned or need, the three steps you just described, what is really being impacted? Just be really real with what is the impact to our business with this change. How long do we think this cash crisis will last? And how long do we have before we run out of cash essentially?
turns.zh: 是的。好的，不错。危机主要有两种：现金危机，即收入突然断掉、投资者撤资或不愿继续支持；产品市场匹配危机，比如竞争对手推出新产品、市场环境变化等。（00:29:28）在现金危机中，假设你意识到现金流比预期少或不足，你刚才提到的三个步骤，真正受影响的核心是什么？我们要实事求是地评估这种变化对业务的影响。现金危机会持续多久？在资金耗尽之前我们还有多长时间？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Yep. And then you need to decide, and then you need to decide on your action and your new plan and maybe it's a new strategy. If all of a sudden I would say if this is about product market fit disappeared, then this is a new strategy. And maybe it's about deciding on extending the run rate or keep on trying or whatever. And this is something that is really interesting. (00:30:17): And we go back to Covid and I look at two of my startups that were in the travel space, one of them is WeSki, and it's essentially the booking.com of ski vacations. And guess what? Covid started. And there was no more ski trips to Europe. Europe were shut down completely. And all the ski areas were shut down. And you know that I'm an avid skier? For me that was a disaster on a personal level. And eventually by the way, what happened is that I was back in Tel Aviv and I was unable to travel to Europe, and it was only somewhere in 2022 that I was able to travel to the US after vaccination and so forth. And in March, 2022, I actually moved myself to Utah to Salt Lake City and I basically say, "No, I'm going to ski every day that I'm not busy." And I skied until the end of the season. (00:31:22): So what happened is that Covid started and we realized that we have major problem. And the problem was actually, the first thing that you face is cancellation because all of a sudden out of very few cancellations per day, you ended up with hundreds of cancellations per day because this is it. And after you dealt with that, then the next question that we ask ourselves, okay, so how bad is it, how long it's going to last? (00:31:54): Now that was supposed to be the first year that we were profitable. So we did not have a lot of cash in the bank because we expected to become profitable this year. And we basically told our ourself, okay, this season is over, next season is not going to happen. We don't know, but we need to plan for something that is going to last longer than that. And then we basically say, okay, how can we deal with it? (00:32:21): Now, because of WeSki had a lot of strategic investors from the travel industry, in the travel industry, they didn't really care about WeSki, they care about their own product. If you are a hotel chain, then guess what? You have no travelers. If you're an airline, guess what? You have no flyers. So anyone in the travel industry suffered from the same problem. And the last thing on earth that they care about is a startup that they invested at. And we realized that, okay, wait a minute, we don't have enough cash to survive for two seasons without revenues, we need to raise additional capital. (00:33:00): Now, no one, no new investor is going to speak with us, because there's no ski, so what are you talking about? And we approached the existing investor, and by the way I'm one of them, and we basically say, "Okay, you know what? We need your help." And everyone told us, "Oh, we are busy. We have other problems to deal with. We have our own problems. I don't see how is that going to become a good investment and so forth." And then we basically decided that, okay, wait a minute, we're going to do a pay to play. (00:33:37): The pay to play is actually sort of forcing new investors at the expense of the existing one. So for example, doing a major down round is sort of pay to play, because if you're not participate your position in the company is going to be diluted severely. And this is what we decided to do. And that was way more complex, I describe that in the book, way more complex than that because we also had safe instruments that we need to convert before we can actually do something like that. And that was really complex. But we ended up doing that. And today the company is actually very successful. (00:34:20): After Covid, we used the time of Covid to actually improve the product, and as soon as Covid was over then we started to grow rapidly. And the company is profitable, is growing rapidly, is actually providing very, very good service to its customers. To a certain extent I would say we ended up getting out of this crisis successfully. (00:34:49): But if you are in the middle of it and you ask yourself, so what are the chances that we will end up being successful? It looks way smaller. Way smaller. So what happened here is that you realize that, okay, this is not forever, so ski is going to come back but we don't know how long and therefore we assume that it's going to be for two seasons until it's coming back, until 2022. And for that we need to adapt. And so we resized the company to be very, very lean and small and we raise just enough capital to survive those two years. And it ended up to be working very well. But in that sense now, if you would ask me how much luck was in there, luck is always good. (00:35:43): I think that I heard ... maybe the most significant real estate developers in New York is Silverstein, and he built the World Trade Center and pretty much everything on the Hudson. And he was asked how he becomes such a successful developer and he said, "Tell you the truth, this is 85% luck and 15% skills and know-how and so forth." And then he was asked if he can change one thing, what exactly it's going to be, and he said, "You know what? I'm going to replace the 15% skills with additional 15% luck." So luck is good. For me luck, I will define luck as opportunity meets readiness. Readiness is up to you; opportunity, not always.
turns.zh:
是的。然后你需要做出决定，确定你的行动方案和新策略。如果突然发现产品市场匹配度消失了，那就需要调整策略。可能需要决定是延长运营周期，还是继续尝试等等。这一点非常有趣。（00:30:17）：让我们回顾新冠疫情期间，我关注了两家旅行领域的初创公司，其中一家是WeSki，实质上是预订滑雪度假的Booking.com。猜猜怎么着？新冠疫情来袭后，欧洲滑雪之旅彻底停摆，所有滑雪场关闭。你知道我是个狂热的滑雪爱好者吧？对个人而言，这简直是灾难。最终，我回到特拉维夫，无法前往欧洲，直到2022年才在接种疫苗后得以返美。2022年3月，我搬到犹他州的盐湖城，告诉自己：“不行，我每天不忙的时候都要去滑雪。”就这样坚持到滑雪季结束。（00:31:22）：新冠疫情爆发后，我们意识到面临重大挑战。首要问题是取消预订量激增——原本每天只有少数取消订单，突然每天数百单取消。应对完这个问题后，我们开始思考：情况有多糟糕？会持续多久？（00:31:54）：本该是我们盈利的第一年，但由于预计今年盈利，银行账户里没有充足现金。我们决定：本季结束，下一季取消。谁知道未来会怎样，但必须为长期应对做准备。于是我们开始探索解决方案。（00:32:21）：由于WeSki有许多来自旅游行业的战略投资者，他们关注的并非WeSki本身，而是自身产品。酒店连锁不接待游客，航空公司没旅客需求。旅游行业普遍面临同样的困境。最后，他们只关心自己投资的初创公司。我们意识到：没有足够现金支撑两个无收入季度，必须筹集额外资金。（00:33:00）：没有新投资者愿意合作，因为滑雪业停滞，他们会问：“你们在说什么？！”我们联系现有投资者（我也是其中之一），请求帮助：“我们需要你们的支持。”结果大家都说：“忙着呢，我们有更重要的事。”这时我们决定采取“付费参与”策略——即以牺牲现有投资者利益为代价引入新资金。例如，大幅降价融资就是典型手段，因为不参与就会导致股权严重稀释。这就是我们选择的策略，远比书中描述的复杂得多，因为我们还面临其他安全性挑战。
因此，我们需要先进行转换，才能真正实现这样的目标。这确实非常复杂。但最终我们还是做到了。如今，这家公司发展得非常成功。（00:34:20）：新冠疫情之后，我们利用那段时间优化了产品，一旦疫情结束，我们就迅速开始了扩张。如今公司盈利能力强劲，增长迅速，还为客户提供了优质的服务。在某种程度上，我认为我们成功走出了这场危机。（00:34:49）：但如果你身处危机中时问自己，成功的几率有多大？看起来微乎其微。非常渺茫。所以关键在于你要意识到，这并非永久的困境，滑雪产业终将复苏，但具体何时回归尚不确定，所以我们假设要等到2022年才会恢复。为此，我们必须调整公司架构，变得极度精简，仅筹集足够维持这两年生存的资金。结果证明这个策略非常有效。谈到运气因素，我认为运气始终是成功的关键。（00:35:43）：我曾听说，纽约最成功的房地产开发商之一是西尔弗斯坦，他建造了世贸中心以及哈德逊河沿岸的诸多地标。当被问及成功秘诀时，他回答：“说实话，成功的85%靠运气，15%靠专业技能和知识。”当被追问如果可以调整比例时，他笑着说：“那就把15%的专业技能换成15%的运气吧。” 所以运气确实很重要。对我而言，运气就是机遇与准备的交汇。准备由你自己把握，而机遇并非总能如期而至。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Beautifully said. I also agree with luck being so core to most people's success, most company's success. But I feel like you're not giving people enough credit for the hard work that's also involved in the skills and timing and stuff.
turns.zh: 说得真好。我也认同运气对大多数人成功至关重要，对大多数公司而言亦是如此。但我觉得你没有充分肯定人们在技能、时机把握等方面的辛勤付出。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: On the readiness.
turns.zh: 关于准备工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's the readiness.
turns.zh: 这就是准备工作。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Of being ready to take advantage of opportunity.
turns.zh: 就是要时刻准备好抓住机遇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes sense. Okay, there's a bunch of stuff I want to dig into here. So one is, and this is something, it's kind of a tangent, but I think it's a core part of your advice on crisis, which is that it's always the founder's fault if things don't work out, even if they're completely out of your control, even if the whole world is changing, it's still your responsibility and your fault if things don't work out.
turns.zh: 有道理。好的，这里有几点我想深入探讨一下。首先，虽说有些跑题，但我认为你关于危机应对的建议中有一条核心观点，即如果事情没有成功，责任始终在创始人身上，即使是完全超出控制范围的情况，即便整个世界都在变，但只要事情没成，责任就归你。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: I wouldn't say fault, I would say responsibility.
turns.zh: 我不会说责任，而是说承担责任。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Responsibility.
turns.zh: 责任。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: It might not end up beautiful, in some cases you will die. But at the end of the day you cannot rely on someone else. The fact that the interest rate is going up and the result is that it's becoming very, very hard to raise capital, the fact that this is industry-wide, so what? You have only one company, you need to make sure that this company is successful. And later on if you fail, then you can rely to then basically say, "This is my excuse, it was not just me." Not just me is not going to help you to become successful. Just me is going to help you to become successful. When you assume responsibility, then you are able to ... you're basically saying, "You know what? I control my own destiny. I'm going to make the decisions and I control my own destiny." When this happens, you increase the likelihood of being successful regardless what happen to the rest of the market, and you don't really care.
turns.zh: 在某些情况下，结果可能不尽如人意，甚至可能导致失败。但归根结底，你不能依赖他人。比如利率上升导致融资变得极其困难，这对整个行业都适用，那又怎样？你只有一家公司，你必须确保这家公司成功。即便失败了，也不能推卸责任，说“这不是我的错”。推卸责任无助于成功，勇于承担责任才能助你成功。当你主动承担责任时，无论市场如何波动，你成功的可能性都会大大增加，而你根本无需在意其他因素。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You also talk along these lines, you have this in your chapter, the section of never give up in a crisis and throughout your journey, this is by far the most important behavior of a startup CEO. Can you just talk about that. Because a lot of times it's like maybe just stop, maybe just give up. You shared one example where it's like I don't want to deal with regulation, other companies, I'm just going to stop. Any advice there, just like, okay, maybe it does make sense just to stop and try to give the investor's money back versus, yeah, it's just part of your job not to give up.
turns.zh: 你也提到过类似观点，在你的章节中，有关在危机中和整个创业历程中永不放弃的部分，这是初创公司CEO最重要的品质。能否谈谈这方面的看法？因为很多时候人们可能会选择停下脚步、放弃。比如你举的例子，面对监管压力和竞争对手的挑战，选择退出。能否给些建议？比如，面对投资者退款要求，是否应该选择停掉项目？毕竟，坚持下去、勇于承担责任才是职责所在。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: I heard of cases that you basically say our underlining assumptions didn't work out and our thesis is wrong and therefore we would like to return the investors their money. But entrepreneurs never give up. And this is the most successful behavior of startup CEO, never give up, always keep on looking for ways to make it work. And so it is going to be a journey of failures, and in particular during crisis, but you still need to keep on trying to make it work even though it's way harder. So never give up is the most important behavior of successful CEO of startup. (00:39:41): The second one, by the way, is making decisions with conviction. This is true for all CEOs or for all companies, not just startups. Now startups, those decisions are probably more frequent and there are a lot of them. But during crisis, all CEOs in the world need to make hard decisions. And you need to make them with conviction because if you don't make them with conviction, then what will happen is that the team is not going to follow. If the team is not going to follow, then you are not going to be successful. (00:40:14): But never give up. You ask entrepreneurs what will happen and they will basically tell you, "No, we keep on fighting." One of my other startups in the travel industry called Oversee, back then they called FairFly. And the CEO told me that a cat might have nine souls. We are a cat in that sense, we have nine souls. And the reason that I know that is that we already died nine times or almost died nine times. And so the reality is that you don't give up, you keep on as long as ... (00:40:56): And for a second I would say, look, there are only two reasons that you would like to give up. One is that your mission is wrong. So the problem disappears. And if the problem disappears, your mission is no longer relevant or no longer valid, and you might want to consider to give up. (00:41:19): The other one is that if the team is not right and you are unable to change it. So you brought toxic investors into the board and they started to control the company and obviously in many cases they create more damage than help. And you're unable to change that anymore, then this is a good reason to give up. (00:41:43): Other than that, never give up. Crisis, not crisis, hardship, no money to pay, no ... anything that might happen, anything that you might want to think that might happen will happen.
turns.zh: 我听说过一些案例，基本上就是说我们的基本假设行不通，我们的论点有误，因此我们想把投资者的钱退还给他们。但创业者从不轻言放弃。这是初创公司CEO最成功的特质——永不言弃，始终寻找让事情运转起来的方法。创业之路注定充满失败，尤其是在危机时刻，但即便再艰难，你也必须继续努力。永不放弃，才是成功初创公司CEO最重要的品质。（00:39:41）：顺便说一句，第二个品质是果断决策。这对所有CEO或所有公司都适用，不只是初创公司。初创公司可能面临更频繁、更多的决策。但在危机时刻，全世界所有的CEO都需要做出艰难抉择。必须果断决策，因为如果不果断，团队就不会跟随；团队不跟随，就注定失败。（00:40:14）：但永不放弃。当你问创业者会怎样时，他们基本都会说：“不，我们会继续战斗。”我旗下一家名为Oversee（当时叫FairFly）的旅游初创公司，其CEO曾告诉我，猫有九条命。我们初创公司就是这样的“猫”，拥有九条命。我之所以知道这一点，是因为我们已经经历了九次濒临倒闭的时刻。现实就是永不放弃，只要……（00:40:56）：暂且说说，你只有两种理由想放弃。一是使命错误。那么问题就消失了。如果问题消失，意味着使命不再相关或有效，或许你就该考虑放弃了。（00:41:19）：另一种情况是团队不合适，你又无力改变。当你引入有毒的投资者进入董事会，他们开始控制公司，显然在很多情况下他们带来的伤害大于帮助。而你再也无法改变这种局面，那这就是放弃的好理由。（00:41:43）：除此之外，永不放弃。无论是危机还是非危机，困难还是资金短缺，任何可能发生的状况，任何你可能预见到可能发生的状况，都会发生。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm excited to chat with Christina Gilbert, the founder of OneSchema, one of our longtime podcast sponsors. Hi Christina.
turns.zh: 很高兴能与OneSchema的创始人克里斯蒂娜·吉尔伯特交流，她是我们长期的播客赞助商之一。嗨，克里斯蒂娜。

turns.speaker: Christina Gilbert
turns.en: Yes, thank you for having me on, Lenny.
turns.zh: 是的，感谢邀请，莱尼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is the latest with OneSchema? I know you now work with some of my favorite companies like Ramp, Vanta, Scale and Watershed. I heard that you just launched a new product to help product teams import CSVs from especially tricky systems like ERPs.
turns.zh: OneSchema的最新动态是什么？我知道你现在与我最喜欢的几家公司合作，比如Ramp、Vanta、Scale和Watershed。听说你们刚推出了一款新产品，帮助产品团队从ERP等复杂系统导入CSV数据。

turns.speaker: Christina Gilbert
turns.en: Yes, so we just launched OneSchema FileFeeds, which allows you to build an integration with any system in 15 minutes as long as you can export a CSV to an SFTP folder. We see our customers all the time getting stuck with hacks and workarounds. And the product teams that we work with don't have to turn down prospects because their systems are too hard to integrate with. We allow our customers to offer thousands of integrations without involving their engineering team at all.
turns.zh: 是的，我们刚推出了OneSchema FileFeeds，只要能将CSV导出到SFTP文件夹，就能在15分钟内与任何系统建立集成。我们经常看到客户被各种临时解决方案和权宜之计困住。而与我们合作的产品团队再也不必因为系统难以集成而拒绝潜在客户了。我们让客户无需动用工程团队就能提供数千种集成服务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I can tell you that if my team had to build integrations like this, how nice would it be to be able to take this off my roadmap and instead use something like OneSchema. And not just to build it but also to maintain it forever.
turns.zh: 我可以告诉你，如果我的团队必须开发这样的集成功能，能把这项任务从路线图中移除，转而使用OneSchema之类的工具，那该有多好啊——不仅能节省开发时间，还能实现长期维护。

turns.speaker: Christina Gilbert
turns.en: Absolutely, Lenny. We've heard so many horror stories of multi-day outages from even just a handful of ad records. We are laser focused on integration reliability to help teams end all of those distractions that come up with integrations. We have a built-in validation layer that stops any bad data from entering your system and OneSchema will notify your team immediately of any data that looks incorrect.
turns.zh: 确实如此，莱尼。我们听过太多因少数广告记录就导致多日停机的恐怖故事。我们正全力提升集成稳定性，帮助团队消除集成带来的种种困扰。我们内置的验证层能阻止错误数据进入系统，一旦发现数据异常，OneSchema会立即通知团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know that importing incorrect data can cause all kinds of pain for your customers and quickly lose their trust. Christina, thank you for joining us. And if you want to learn more, head on over to oneschema.co. That's oneschema.co. (00:43:30): This idea of never give up, it's very similar to Dalton Caldwell was on the podcast, he's a partner at YC, and his whole ... he has a famous talk, I guess, at YC, and this was the title of this podcast episode, is just don't die. That's his main advice to a startup, just don't die.
turns.zh: 我知道导入错误数据会让客户痛不欲生，信任感瞬间崩塌。克里斯蒂娜，感谢你的参与。如果想了解更多信息，请访问oneschema.co。（00:43:30）：永不言弃的理念和达尔顿·考德威尔在播客上的观点非常相似。他是YC的合伙人，曾在YC做过一场著名的演讲，这次播客的标题就是“别死”。这是他对初创企业的核心建议——永不放弃。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Never give up.
turns.zh: 永不放弃。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Never give up.
turns.zh: 永不放弃。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: You might die by the way, you might die, you'll never give up.
turns.zh: 说实话，你可能会死掉，你肯定会死掉，但你永远不会放弃。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Then be reborn. And to be clear, the way a startup dies is they run out of money, is that the simplest way to think about that?
turns.zh: 然后重生。说白了，初创企业死亡的方式就是资金耗尽，这是最简单直观的解释吧？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: That's the only way that they die. By the way, all the companies in the world, they are unable to pay their bills and therefore they die.
turns.zh: 这是它们死亡的唯一原因。顺便说一句，世界上所有公司都会遇到资金短缺的问题，最终走向灭亡。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And many of the tactics you share is just ways to not run out of money. Oftentimes it involves down rounds, creating strange cap structures just to keep it alive, losing equity percentage just to keep it going, that's part of the job basically, and that's what you have to deal with.
turns.zh: 你分享的许多策略都是为了避免资金枯竭。比如降低融资轮次、设计奇怪的股权结构来维持生存、让渡股权比例以维持运营——这些本质上都是生存之道，也是初创者必须面对的挑战。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: In many cases, we had to engage the employees, "No, we don't have cash." So what we did is that we diluted all shareholders in order to give employees way more equity. So five times more equity than they had before. And we told them, we need you to trust us and believe in the cause and believe in our ability to recover. And if we don't, then everyone loses. But if we do, then everyone wins big time. And so this will be a way to actually reengage employees if you are unable to pay them their regular pay. And that was the case in most of the startups that almost run out of cash. (00:45:08): Occasionally you can do, if you will tell me that you're going to run out of cash next month and therefore you need to shut down, I would like to imagine that you have at least six more month of run rate. You don't know that, but this is through leadership. So you basically tell your people, "Stay with me, you believed in the cause, you believed in my leadership, I still believe in the cause and I still believe in you. And maybe we are going to have some hard time, maybe we are going to have some month that unable to pay, but eventually we will get out of that." And in many cases, most people will stay. (00:45:55): Now, leadership, you don't build leadership during crisis, you might, but in particular you build leadership through transparency, through recognitions of your team, through actually putting your team as the top priority. At the end of the day, you are going to be successful if your team delivers. And in order for the team to deliver, then they need you to trust them to deliver.
turns.zh: 很多情况下，我们不得不对员工说：“不，我们没有现金。” 所以我们的做法是，稀释所有股东的股权，以便为员工提供更多股权——比他们之前多五倍。我们告诉他们，我们需要你们信任我们，相信我们的事业，相信我们能渡过难关。如果不这样做，大家都会输。但如果我们成功了，每个人都会大获全胜。因此，如果无法支付员工正常薪酬，这将是重新激发员工积极性的有效方法。（00:45:08）：偶尔你可能会说，你下个月就会面临资金告急，因此需要关闭公司。我希望你至少还有六个月的正常运营周期。虽然你自己也不确定，但这需要领导力来体现。所以你要告诉员工：“和我一起坚持，你们曾相信这项事业，相信我的领导力，我现在依然坚信这一切。也许我们会经历艰难时期，也许会有无法支付薪酬的月份，但最终我们会走出困境。” 在大多数情况下，大多数员工都会留下来。（00:45:55）：说到领导力，你不能在危机中临时培养，可能可以，但关键在于通过透明度、对团队的认可，以及将团队置于首要位置来培养领导力。归根结底，如果团队能交付成果，你才能成功。而要想团队交付成果，就需要你信任他们能做到。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is really powerful advice and I want to spend a little more time here, which is keeping people on board and engaged and motivated through a crisis. So this kind of almost script you just shared is really great. Is there anything else that you found useful or any advice you could share for helping a founder keep the team on board, keep people excited, driven? These words you shared I think is a really good example, is there anything else?
turns.zh: 这些建议真的非常有力，我想在这里多花点时间讨论如何在危机中留住员工、激发他们的积极性和动力。你刚刚分享的这种近乎标准的做法真的很棒。还有其他你觉得有用的建议，或者能帮助创始人留住团队、保持员工热情和动力的方法吗？你分享的这些话，我认为就是一个很好的例子，你还有其他建议吗？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: So during crisis, people will appreciate more than anything else transparency. And if you hide information from them, then they would leave, they don't trust you anymore. But if there is a crisis, and look, if there is a crisis then everyone knows that there is a crisis, it's not surprising for anyone. And this is where they expect your leadership the most. This is where they expect you to be there for them. And tell them that this is what we're going to do. And if ABC happens, then we will be successful. And if it's not, then we will die. And I want you to believe that we can deliver A, B and C, and I want you to stay here for that part of the journey. And this is really, really dramatic, this is perhaps the most important part. Look, during crisis, the team is the one that is going to take you out of the crisis, and you need them more than ever. And guess what? They need you.
turns.zh: 在危机期间，人们最看重的是透明度。如果你隐瞒信息，他们就会离开，不再信任你。但如果真的遇到危机，每个人都知道有危机发生，这对任何人来说都不意外。这正是他们最期待你的领导力的时候，也是他们最需要你支持的时候。告诉他们，我们要这样做。如果ABC发生了，我们就能成功。如果不成功，我们就会失败。我希望你们相信我们能做到A、B、C，我希望你们能在这段旅程中留下来。这真的非常重要，可能是最重要的部分。看，在危机中，团队会带你走出困境，你比以往任何时候都更需要他们。猜猜怎么着？他们也同样需要你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When you talk about being transparent and open about everything, what's an example of just how far you recommend people go? Because you could just be like, here's all of our data and metrics and numbers, here's what our investors are emailing me. How real do you recommend people get? I know it's hard to just summarize in a couple sentences, but what's a good way to illustrate that?
turns.zh: 当你谈到对一切保持透明和开放时，你建议人们能做到什么程度？因为你可能只是说，所有数据、指标和数字都在这里，这是投资者发给我的邮件。你建议人们要多真实？我知道很难用几句话概括，但有什么好的方法可以说明这一点？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: So number one, don't sugarcoat. So you basically you don't need to share all the feedbacks from all the investors. You can tell them, "Look, I met dozens of investors in the last couple of weeks and they're all saying no." Or we had a signed term sheet and the investor disappeared. Okay, that's fine. It is what it is. Look, the fact that it's ugly, if you don't tell that it's ugly, it's still ugly. (00:48:49): And so I would share the essence. And if we have metrics, then what I would like to do is believe that everyone is aware of the metrics, of the key metrics of the company. This is something that in general I would say, "Oh, in the lobby of the office, we should have the key metrics displayed for everyone to understand this is what we stand for, this is how well we are executing anyhow." And so when they will see the numbers drop, they know that the numbers drop. And this is something that I will in general I would say, look, key metrics, they should be shared anyhow. And so in particular during crisis, we should keep on sharing them. Definitely not hiding information. So if you have a major customer leave or investor disappear or we are unable to sign a term sheet. And so this is the highlight, this is the major issue. And the details themselves, it's less critical. Now if people ask, then answer. If someone ask, "Okay, so how many investors have you met?" I'd say no, then start counting, 37, be specific.
turns.zh: 首先，别粉饰太平。也就是说，你不必把所有投资者的反馈都和盘托出。你可以告诉他们：“听着，我过去几周见了数十位投资者，他们全都拒绝了。” 或者我们签了投资意向书，结果投资方却消失了。没关系，现实就是如此。说实话，事情本质上就是糟糕的，如果你不说出来，它依然糟糕。（00:48:49）所以我会把关键信息分享出去。如果我们有数据指标，那么我想强调的是，要确保每个人都了解公司的核心指标。总的来说，我会说：“哦，办公室大厅应该展示这些关键指标，让大家明白这是我们的核心目标，说明我们的执行情况如何。” 当数据下滑时，他们会知道数字在下跌。总的来说，我认为关键指标应该随时共享，尤其是在危机时期，更要坚持透明。绝对不能隐瞒信息。比如有大客户流失、投资方消失、无法签署投资意向书等情况，这些都是关键问题。具体细节则没那么重要。有人问起时，就如实回答。比如有人问：“你见了多少位投资者？” 你可以说没有，然后开始逐一列举，37位，要准确无误。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a great answer. I want to come back to something you said that I think is so important but so hard, which is to act fast. If I was a founder, something changes in the market, it's easy to say, "Okay, you need to cut burn, you need go raise money, down round." It's so hard to do, to lay people off, to do all these challenging things for your company. Can you again just help people understand why it's so important to act fast? You talked about optionality goes away. Just like what actually happens there if you don't?
turns.zh: 这回答得太棒了。我想再回归到你提到的另一个至关重要却又极难做到的点——快速行动。如果我是创始人，市场环境发生变化时，人们很容易说：“好吧，你得削减开支、融资、降轮次。” 但实际做起来却异常艰难，比如裁员、处理公司面临的各种挑战。你能再帮大家理解一下，为什么快速行动如此重要吗？你提到一旦失去了选择权，那具体会怎样？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: So I'll give you an example. So let's say that you are almost run out of cash and you believe that you're going to raise capital in the next two month. And if not, then you run out of cash. One of the things that you might want to do is extend the run rate. One other thing that you might want to do is actually tell the people that we will be running out of cash in two month. And number one, I want you to help me even if we run out of cash because there are good chances that we eventually will be able to raise capital and recover that. And number two, in order to get your support and belief in the company I am going to offer you more equity. So, the more equity is something that I will do twice, once today, once you realize that this is going to be challenging, and then again if we need to ask people to reduce their salary or do something dramatic around that. (00:51:59): And the first one is actually preventive action. So you share the know-how, you share the challenges that we are going to face. And you demonstrate generosity not out of you have to, but you demonstrate that. And then you essentially dramatically increase their loyalty and their commitment. And when you will need them, they will be there. So this is one example. (00:52:35): The other example is about calculating end of cash. And this is really, really important. So let's say that you have run rate of X month, six month. If you reduce burn by 50% today, then you simply increase your run rate to a year. If you don't do it today and you wait three more month, then you only can do that for the ... so the first three month you burn the same way that you did up until now, and now you reduce that to half, so you have six more month, total of nine month. If you decided today that you need 12 month, and you don't act today, you will never have 12 month. (00:53:32): Now, is that the only way to do that? No, it's not the only way, but it's one of the ways that by the way most companies will do. So they will reduce burn rate today in order to extend the run rate. Is that going to be more helpful? Don't know. Really depending on the case. (00:53:53): If you had asked me if you reduce the burn rate, increase the run rate, so now you have 12 month to raise new capital, is that going to have higher likelihood of remaining with the current plan and growth and raise capital within six month? I don't know that. But this is exactly the decision that you need to make.
turns.zh:
接下来，我举个例子。假设你手头现金即将告罄，并且预计未来两个月内能筹集到资金。如果未能成功，你的现金流将耗尽。此时，你或许会考虑延长现金流转周期，或者直接告知员工我们将在两个月内面临资金短缺的情况。首先，我希望即便现金告罄，你们仍能协力共渡难关，因为很有可能我们最终能成功融资并弥补资金缺口。其次，为获取员工对公司的支持和信心，我将向你们提供更多股权激励。具体而言，我会在两个关键节点实施激励措施：一是当下，二是当我们不得不削减员工薪资或采取其他激进措施时。  
（00:51:59）：第一种策略属于预防性措施。你需要坦诚分享面临的挑战，展现出慷慨之举——并非迫于无奈，而是出于真诚。这样做能显著提升员工忠诚度与凝聚力。在你需要他们时，他们必将挺身而出。这就是一个典型案例。  
（00:52:35）：另一个案例涉及现金流转周期计算，这至关重要。假设你当前现金流转周期为X个月或6个月。若今日将消耗率削减50%，则可将流转周期延长至一年。若拖延至三个月后，只能将周期延长至9个月。如果你今日决定需12个月融资却未采取行动，最终将永远无法实现12个月的融资期限。  
（00:53:32）：这是否唯一可行之策？并非唯一，但多数公司都会选择这种策略——即刻降低消耗率以延长流转周期。这种方法是否更有效？难以断定，需视具体情况而定。  
（00:53:53）：若你询问：削减消耗率、延长流转周期后，现在有12个月筹集新资金，成功延续现有增长计划并在6个月内完成融资的概率是否更高？这难以确定。但这正是你必须做出的决策。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really great way of putting it. Just the math means the leverage you have now to extend runway is so much higher the sooner you make the decision. And the key, just going back to your algorithm of deciding if we need to act in this way quickly, is first think about what's being impacted, then how long is this impact going to last, and then how long do I have before you run out of money. And those questions is your advice for deciding, do we let people go now, do we raise money now.
turns.zh: 你这么说太到位了。从数学角度看，你越早做出决策，就能越有效地延长现金流转周期。关键在于，判断是否需要迅速采取行动的算法是：首先思考哪些方面会受到影响，其次影响会持续多久，最后你还有多少时间才能耗尽资金。这些问题就是你判断是否该立即裁员或融资的依据。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: There is always, by the way, there is always alternative for let people go. In general, I would say letting people go is probably better than reducing salary for everyone. But let's say that you need cost reduction of 30%. One of the options is let 30% of the people go. Another option is actually reduce salary by 30% for everyone. And it's going to have the same impact. Not exactly, the same impact on the balance sheet and on the P&L, but not necessarily on the organization. If the organization feels that they are committed to each other, they will prefer the second way. If this is more of individuals, then obviously they will prefer the first way. (00:55:45): Is there a different way? What about if management gives up on their salary? That might make the same impact. And definitely demonstration of leadership. And by the way, increasing the commitment of the rest of the organization. (00:56:06): So in that sense, I would say there are multiple ways of reducing the cost. But in general, this is always about impacting people. If you look at the startup and you look at the budget, 70% of the budget is people, maybe 75% of the budget is people. Everything else is nickels and dimes. If you're going to tell me, "Oh no, we are going to start the supply of coffee to the office and this is how we are going to reduce cost." No, this is how you create dissatisfaction with the team and you would reduce costs because some people would leave because of that, not because of lack of coffee, but because of inability to determine and to make hard decisions. So end of the day, if you need to reduce costs that means people.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，总是有让员工离职的替代方案。总的来说，我认为让员工离职可能比为所有人降薪更好。但假设你需要削减30%的成本。一种选择是让30%的员工离职。另一种选择是为所有人降薪30%。这两种方案对财务报表和损益表的影响相同，但对组织的影响不尽相同。如果组织成员彼此忠诚，他们会更倾向于后者。如果更多是以个人为单位，那显然他们会更青睐前者。 （00:55:45）：有没有其他办法？如果管理层放弃自己的薪资呢？这可能会产生相同的效果，而且无疑能彰显领导力。顺便说一句，还能增强组织内其他成员的忠诚度。 （00:56:06）：所以从这个角度来看，我认为削减成本的方法多种多样。但总的来说，这始终涉及到对员工产生影响。如果你看看初创公司的预算，70%的预算用于人员成本，75%的预算可能都用于人员成本。其他一切都是零零碎碎的小钱。如果你跟我说：“哦，不，我们要开始为办公室供应咖啡，这样就能削减成本了。” 不，这只会让团队不满，最终削减成本是因为有人因此离职，不是因为缺咖啡，而是因为缺乏决断力和勇于做艰难决定的能力。所以归根结底，如果你需要削减成本，那就意味着要裁员。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was really good advice and really good set of options to consider versus laying people off. So most of what we've been talking about right now has been the cash crisis route. We've spent a little time on the product market fit crisis route. But I want to spend a little more time there. So for the cash crisis route, you have these kind of three questions and then it's like, cool, this will tell you how quickly to act and how severely to make cuts. In the product market fit route, is it essentially if you've lost product market fit, it's to pivot, is that basically the question? And then it's a question of where to pivot and what to do?
turns.zh: 这真是很棒的建议，也是考虑如何替代裁员的绝佳方案。我们目前讨论的大多是现金危机路线。我们花了一点时间讨论了产品市场契合度危机路线。但我想在这方面再多花点时间。对于现金危机路线，你会遇到这三个问题，然后就能判断出应该多快采取行动、多大程度地削减开支。对于产品市场契合度路线，本质上就是如果你失去了产品市场契合度，就要转型，这对吧？然后问题就变成该转型到哪里去，以及该怎么做？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: So the first question is, am I still relevant? And probably the answer is no. And then the next question that you basically say, "Okay, do I want to pivot?" And for that I will say, "If I would start today, is this is what I'm going to do?" And if the answer is yes, then do it. (00:57:54): Now in many cases you say, "Oh, wait a minute, I already have the organization and I already have money in the bank and this is what I'm going to do instead." I wouldn't necessarily do that. The way that I would look at it is different. Because the other alternative is basically say, "Wait a minute, all of my underlining assumptions have gone, they are wrong." I lost product market fit. The value proposition that I had is wrong or is no longer valid or no longer relevant. And therefore I need to start from scratch. Do I really have the assets to become successful on the new path? (00:58:44): And the assets could be technology that you already developed, could be the team that you already built, could be the know-how that you have in that specific market that gives you a significant advantage. And if any of those is really, really significant, then it's possible that you want to pivot. Pivot basically say major fuck up, all of our underlining assumptions have gone. (00:59:13): And because everything else, if it's not, then that's part of the journey of failure. If you'll tell me, "Oh, we tried this product or we tried this feature and didn't work," then this journey of fail. This is going to be your journey. (00:59:27): But once you figure out product market fit, if it disappears, then pivot is one option, shutting down is another option. And for shutting down, there are two things that you need to ask yourself. Do I have the energy to keep on going? Maybe you basically say, "I spent the last seven years trying to do that and now it's gone and you know what? I need some time off." (00:59:53): And the other one is that do I really have the assets to become dramatically successful? Pontera is one of my startups that I started back in 2012. And back then we called that FeeX. And we were dealing with financial fees in Israel and we were actually pretty successful. And then we decided, okay, wait a minute, Israel is a small market, let's move to the US. And we moved to the US. And one day the CEO came to me and said, "Look, we need to focus, I cannot do both, so we need to pivot." And we stopped the Israeli operation completely in order to focus all of our effort on the US operation. And then we realized that the nature of the beast is different and therefore we need to re-look for product market fit. And eventually we found that with the regulations of the Obama administration, and that was our product back in 2016 or 17. (01:00:59): And then the administration have changed and now it's going to change again. And they changed the regulation. And overnight we figured out that ... And we were actually on being a successful path. And we had to reinvent ourself. Now, what we basically said is, "Look, we have the energy to keep on going, we have something, a thesis that we believe might be relevant for us. We have the technology that can serve the thesis and we have enough cash to try it out." And we went back to the board and we offered them two options. Number one, we give you your money back. And number two, this is what we're going to try. (01:01:43): And the interesting part is that investors don't want their money back. They did not invest in order to have their money back, they invest in order to make a significant impact. And obviously they don't want to go back to their investors and tell them, guess what? And so we had all the support to keep trying something else. And since 2018, we are actually being pretty successful on this path. And all of a sudden, company is 12 years old, and we pivoted twice. And now we are end of the day helping Americans to retire richer. Helping financial advisors to support you on your 401k plans, on retirement saving plans. And the result is pretty significant. So this company is on a path of being successful, but we almost died twice. (01:02:44): And look, all the CEOs in the world, if you would ask them, have you nearly died already? And they will tell you yes. And then the next question would be how many times? And they will tell you multiple times. And if they're not, that means that they're simply too early on their journey.
turns.zh:
首个问题是，我是否还具竞争力？答案很可能是"不"。接下来你会问："好吧，我要转型吗？"对此我的回答是，如果今天重头再来，我还会选择这样做吗？如果答案是肯定的，那就行动吧。

（00:57:54）：在许多情况下，你会想："等等，我已经有了组织架构，手头还有资金，这次转型换个方向如何？"但我不建议这样做。我的看法不同。因为另一种选择就是承认："等等，我们所有的基本假设都崩塌了，它们都是错的。"我们失去了产品与市场的契合度，原有的价值主张不再适用或失去意义。这时就必须从零开始。新道路上我们是否具备成功的资产？

（00:58:44）：这些资产可能是已开发的技术、组建的团队，或在特定市场积累的专业知识。只要其中任何一项至关重要，转型就值得考虑。转型本质上就是承认重大失败，承认所有基本假设都已失效。

（00:59:13）：而当产品与市场契合度消失时，转型是选择之一，关闭项目是另一种选择。关闭项目前，需审视两点：是否有精力继续前行？比如你会说："过去七年努力无果，现在一切归零，何不休息？"

（00:59:53）：另一个问题是，是否具备在新领域大获成功的资产？Pontera是我2012年创立的初创公司，当时名为FeeX。我们专注以色列金融费用领域，取得了不错成绩。后决定进军美国市场，但美国市场比以色列小得多。我们关闭以色列业务，将全部精力投入美国市场。然而发现市场性质不同，必须重新寻找产品与市场的契合点，最终借助奥巴马政府的监管政策（2016-2017年）成功转型。

（01:00:59）：如今政策变更，我们又面临调整。回顾历史，我们的决策基于三点：有精力继续前行，有可行的商业假设，拥有支撑假设的技术。最终向董事会提出两个方案：退款或继续尝试。幸运的是，投资者更看重影响力而非退款。
想回到投资者面前，告诉他们，猜猜怎么着？于是我们获得了全力支持，继续尝试其他方向。自2018年以来，我们在这条道路上其实取得了不俗的成绩。如今，公司已走过12个年头，我们经历了两次转型。如今，我们致力于帮助美国人实现财富自由，助力财务顾问为客户的401(k)计划和退休储蓄方案提供支持。成效显著。这家公司如今正走在成功之路上，可我们曾两次濒临倒闭。（01:02:44）看看全球所有CEO，如果你问他们，是否曾经历过九死一生？他们都会回答是。而接下来的问题会是：有过几次？他们都会回答不止一次。若他们否认，那就意味着他们还处在创业初期。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such an important point. It came up, I just had Toby from Shopify on the podcast, and he said exactly the same thing. That just like the number of times Shopify almost died, people have no idea. It's important to know, that's very common.
turns.zh: 这一点太重要了。我刚在播客上采访了Shopify的托比，他也说了完全一样的话。Shopify差点倒闭的次数多得超乎想象，但人们对此却知之甚少。这一点很重要，要知道这种情况其实很常见。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Yeah. And I'm a good friend with Harley Finkelstein, the president of Shopify, and he told ... we exchanged horror stories about nearly dying. And we are still here.
turns.zh: 是啊。我和Shopify的总裁哈利·芬克尔斯坦是好朋友，他跟我说……我们还互相分享了差点倒闭的恐怖故事。不过我们现在依然坚守阵地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just never give up. To double down on this pivot point real quick. So the things you should look at to help you decide if a pivot is a good idea, you shared, you have some tech that might be helpful in this new direction, you have a team that's really well suited to this new idea or you have some knowledge. Is there anything else, just like what's that list of things you should look at to see, to come up with ideas/decide this is a good idea for us to pursue?
turns.zh: 永远不要轻言放弃。再快速回顾一下这次转型策略的关键点。你提到要判断转型是否可行的关键点包括：是否有适配新方向的技术、是否有适合新方向的团队、是否有相关知识。还有其他需要考虑的因素吗？比如说，要想出新点子/决定是否值得推进，应该重点关注哪些方面？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: So going back to basic, but now you are already running, so you probably have already validated the problem or the value proposition. About pivoting, so when you start you think that, okay, I have this brilliant idea. And what I really encourage people is first of all, go and validate the problem, speak with people, understand their perception of the problem. And only then start to think about the solution. Now, this is still not the case in most startups. And this is fall in love with the problem, not the solution. And for a few reasons, and maybe number one reason is, look, entrepreneurship journey is about creating value. Simplest way to create value, seel a product, that's it, simplest way. And I like simple. (01:04:50): But then in addition, when you focus on the problem, then the problem is going to serve as the north star of your journey. And when you have a north star, you're going to make less deviation from the course and increase the likelihood of being successful. But by and large, your story is going to be way more compelling. If we will be here in 2007, and I will tell you that I'm going to build an AI crowdsourced based navigation system, you're going to say, "Oh yeah, very interesting," But you don't care. If I will tell you I'm going to help you to avoid traffic jams, then you do care. When your customer care, they want you to be successful. And when they want you to be successful, they are going to help you to become successful. (01:05:31): And so this is going back into pivoting the same way, first of all, validate what's your value proposition, what's the problem you're going to solve. Now, in most cases you already validated that because you in the market for some years and you had dialogues with customers and you already realized that. And maybe you already told yourself, you know what? In my next startup this is what I'm going to do. And so it's possible that you already validated. And if you haven't, then this is exactly the time to revalidate the value proposition. So this is the first thing that you need to do. (01:06:06): And then the second thing that you want to do is ask yourself, do I really have a significant advantage here? Do I really have the team, the technology, the know-how to make a leap from here and really lead the market? (01:06:22): And then the other part of it is, okay, do I have the energy and the passion to go and do it all over again? Because this is going back to square one, trying to figure out product market fit and then figuring out business model and then figuring out growth and so forth. So the entire journey from scratch. And if you answer yes to all of those, so you have the very significant value proposition and you think that you have something that is going to accelerate you dramatically because of the know-how, the technology, the team, then the next thing that you're going to do is validate it with the team. (01:07:05): In your underlining assumptions the team is going to continue. Maybe, maybe not. This is exactly the time that you would like to validate that. And the way that you're going to validate that is you basically say to them, "Guess what? We are fucked. Our underlining assumptions are no longer valid. And this is our new opportunity and we can go this path or we can die." And let's see what people, if they believe in the new path, then this is a good idea. (01:07:36): In many cases, by the way, it's possible that the new path will come from them. They're the one that are closer to the customers, they're the one that are closer to the technology. They're the one that are probably know better than you if this new path is actually valid or not. And if this is the case, then you go and do it. (01:07:56): The last one that you want to ... Look, even if you don't have the money for it, let's say that you don't have plenty of cash in the bank, go back to the investors and go back to raise capital because now you actually have a very significant advantage. You already have a technology, you already have a team, you already have the know-how, you are already second time entrepreneur because pivot is like restarting from scratch or you are already multiple times entrepreneur, so you are way more attractive today than when you were a few years back. And so go back to existing investors and new investors and raise more capital for this new journey.
turns.zh:
回到基础问题，但既然你已经在运营阶段，或许你已经验证过问题或价值主张了。关于调整战略，当你刚起步时，总会觉得“我有个绝妙的点子”。我真正想鼓励大家的是：首先去验证问题，去和用户交流，理解他们对问题的认知。然后再去思考解决方案。但大多数初创公司都做不到这一点。这就是“爱上问题而非解决方案”的典型案例。原因有几个，其中最重要的是：创业的本质是创造价值，最简单的创造价值方式就是卖出产品，仅此而已。我喜欢简单明了的路径。（01:04:50）但除此之外，专注于问题本身会让它成为你前进的北极星。当你有了明确的方向，偏离航线的可能性就会大大降低，成功的概率也会大大提升。更重要的是，你的故事会更有说服力。假如2007年我们告诉你，我们要开发一个基于AI众包的导航系统，你可能会说“哦，有意思”。但你不会在意。若我们说要帮助你避开交通拥堵，你就会感兴趣。当客户关心你的成功时，也会助你一臂之力。（01:05:31）这同样适用于战略调整：首先验证你的价值主张和要解决的问题。在多数情况下，你可能已经验证过了，因为你已经在市场上耕耘数年，与客户对话后发现了方向。或许你甚至已经暗下决心：“下次创业我要这么做。”如果尚未验证，那么此时正是重新验证价值主张的最佳时机。这是首要任务。（01:06:06）接下来要问自己：我是否真的拥有显著的竞争优势？我是否具备团队、技术和专业知识来引领市场？（01:06:22）再看是否有精力和热情从头再来：从产品市场匹配到商业模式，再到增长策略，整个过程都要重头再来。若对以上问题都回答是，那么你就拥有了极具价值的商业主张，并且相信凭借技术、团队等资源能大幅加速发展。此时你需要做的就是与团队共同验证。（01:07:05）在核心假设上，团队可能会继续支持，也可能不然。此时正是验证假设的关键时刻。验证方式就是坦诚地告诉他们：“猜猜看？我们完蛋了。原有假设失效了。现在有新机遇，我们要么走新路，要么死掉。” 看看团队是否愿意相信新路径。（01:07:36）许多情况下，新路径可能来自团队本身。他们更贴近客户，更熟悉技术，拥有更敏锐的洞察力。
很可能比你更清楚这条新路径是否切实可行。如果确实如此，那就大胆尝试。（01:07:56）：最后一点，你需要……听着，即便你手头资金不足，比如银行存款不充足，也别犹豫。回到投资者面前，重新融资，因为现在你具备了极大的优势——你已掌握核心技术，组建了专业团队，积累了宝贵经验。无论你是二次创业者（因为转型相当于从零开始）还是多次创业者，相较于几年前的自己，如今的你显然更具吸引力。所以，勇敢地向现有投资者和新投资者寻求更多资金，为新征程注入活力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like this algorithm. I was writing it down as you're talking. So basically when you're deciding to pivot, looking for opportunities to pivot, step one is find a problem, validate there's a problem that exists. Step two is figure out if you have the tech, team or know-how that gives you an advantage to win at solving this problem. Then ask yourself, do you have the passion and energy to be spending your life and the many number of years attacking this problem? Then validate your team, wants to also go after this problem. And then check with your investors and try to get money to fund you going after this problem.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个算法。你讲的时候我一直在记笔记。所以基本上，当你决定转型、寻找转型机会时，第一步是发现问题，验证问题是否真实存在。第二步是评估你是否拥有技术、团队或专业知识，能让你在解决这个问题时占据优势。然后问自己，你是否有激情和精力，将一生和多年时光投入到攻克这个问题中？接着要验证你的团队是否也愿意追寻这个目标。最后，咨询投资人，争取资金支持来推进这个项目。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: And I like this order now. Some people will tell you, "Oh, my order is different." And I'm not saying if this is the right thing or the wrong thing, but I think that ... One of the reason that I say this is the order is, look, when you validate the problem and the value proposition, even if you don't have the passion, if it's been validated, your passion will be built up. Because then you speak with potential customers and you tell them, "This is what I'm thinking of doing and this is how it's going to help you." They will say, "Yes, I need that. Can you do it tomorrow?" Then all of a sudden you get excited about it. (01:10:05): And usually when I speak about consumers then I tell people, look, when you go and speak about the problem, if the answer that you are going to get is, "Oh, I know someone that had this problem," don't follow this path. If they will tell you, "No, no, no, no, no, this is not the problem, the problem is," and they will give you their version of the problem, this is where you want to follow that. To a certain point, if you speak with enough people, you would have the sense that you are being sent on a mission. And this is where your passion is going to go through the roof. And so don't start with the passion, let the passion be built.
turns.zh: 现在我喜欢这个顺序了。有些人会说，“哦，我的顺序不一样。”我不是说这是对是错，但我认为……我之所以说这个顺序重要的原因之一是，看，当你验证问题和价值主张时，即使你没有激情，如果问题被验证了，你的激情也会被激发。因为当你与潜在客户交流，告诉他们，“这是我想做的，它会如何帮助你。”他们会说，“是的，我需要这个。你明天能做吗？”然后突然间你就兴奋起来了。（01:10:05）：通常当我谈到消费者时，我会告诉人们，看，当你去谈论问题时，如果对方回答，“哦，我认识一个有过这个问题的人。”别走这条路。如果他们会告诉你，“不，不，不，不，不，这不是问题所在，问题是……”，然后他们会给你他们版本的问题，这才是你应该追随的。到了一定程度，如果你与足够多的人交流，你会感觉自己被派去执行一项任务。这时你的激情会爆棚。所以别从激情开始，让激情自然产生。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I totally feel that. I have friends who started this company Zip, which is a procurement, a really good procurement platform. And I don't know if they were growing up wanting to be building a business that helps procurement experiences be better. And they pivoted six times before they picked this idea. But through that, I think found how big of a deal this was and how much happier people can be in their day to day with a better product and got excited about it. And now that's what they're building.
turns.zh: 我完全能理解这一点。我有朋友创办了Zip公司，这是一个非常好的采购平台。我不知道他们是否从小就想创建一个能改善采购体验的企业。在他们选择这个想法之前，他们转了六次方向。但通过这个过程，我认为他们发现了这个问题的重大意义，以及人们在日常生活中使用更好的产品时能获得多大的快乐，并为此而兴奋不已。现在这就是他们正在打造的东西。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: The best thing happen when you try to validate a problem is that you speak with someone and they will tell you in a very strong emotional word, "I hate that," or something like that. Yeah, this is exactly what you're looking for, you're looking for something that people will engage emotionally and with strong emotions.
turns.zh: 验证问题时最美好的事情就是，你和某人交流，他们会用非常强烈的情感语言对你说：“我讨厌这样。”或者类似的话。是的，这正是你所寻找的，你要寻找能让人们产生情感共鸣、情绪激动的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Someone once described it as you want to look for their pupils to dilate when you tell them, when you talk about this problem.
turns.zh: 有人曾把它描述为，当你向他们描述这个问题时，他们瞳孔放大。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There was a quote I wrote down as you were talking earlier that I think is really great. It's kind of a framework for ... the way you used it is to help you pick which direction to go. But I think it's a useful framework in general for companies and founders is ask yourself, if I were to start today, what would I have done and what would I do if I were to start this company again today? I think that's such a powerful thing to always think about even when everything's going great.
turns.zh: 之前你讲话时，我记下了一句话，我觉得这句话非常棒。这算是一个框架……你用它的方式是帮助你选择前进的方向。但我认为这个框架对公司和创始人来说总体上很有用，就是问自己：如果我今天重新开始，我会怎么做？如果我今天重新创办这家公司，我又会怎么做？我觉得即使一切顺利，也要经常思考这个问题。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: I agree. Today is the first day of the rest of your life. And this is pretty much everything in your life. So ask yourself, knowing what I know today, would I do something different? Now, if the answer is yes, then do something different today. Don't wait until next life or next company or next relationship or next something. If you basically know today that you should be doing something different, then change.
turns.zh: 我同意。今天是你余生第一天。人生中的一切都如此重要。所以问问自己，知道了今天所知的信息，你会不会做些不同的事？如果答案是肯定的，那就从今天开始行动。别等到下辈子、下一家公司、下一段感情或者下一个什么时候。如果你今天就知道应该做出改变，那就立刻行动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that's extra important because somebody will do that probably and compete with you and put you out of business, and it's better that you do that first.
turns.zh: 我觉得这点尤为重要，因为很可能会有人来竞争，迫使你退出市场，而你最好能先行一步。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: But this is true for everything in your life. Look, if you are working in a place and you are not happy and you suffer there, then I would say ... The guidance that I give to my children is very simple. If you're not happy at your working place, then ask yourself, is there something that I can do to change that? Then try to change that for the next three month. If you're unable to change that, then leave. You don't deserve to be unhappy. And you need to control your own destiny. For me, quitting your job, do you know what it means? You fire your own job boss, that's what it means. You fire your boss by quitting, that's it.
turns.zh: 但这适用于你人生中的一切。看，如果你在某个地方工作不开心、备受煎熬，那我会说……我给孩子的建议很简单。如果工作环境让你不开心，那就问问自己，有什么办法能改变现状？然后在接下来的三个月里努力改变。如果实在无法改变，那就离开。你不该忍受不开心，你得掌控自己的命运。对我来说，辞职意味着什么？就是你解雇了自己的老板，就是这么回事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's empowering, I like that. Okay, just, okay, two more questions. One is I want to close the loop on the Waze story. So you talked about how Google launched, a competitor basically, free turn-by-turn directions, that was the business you were building and you essentially had to change direction. What did you actually do, how did you decide and realize this?
turns.zh: 这很赋权，我喜欢这种态度。好的，再问两个问题。第一个是关于Waze的故事的收尾。你提到谷歌推出了竞争产品，免费的实时导航服务，而这正是你们当时在开发的产品，最终不得不改变方向。具体你们做了什么？是如何做出决定并意识到这一点的？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: We didn't change. Back in 2010, we were simply not good enough, we were still in the product market fit iterations and iterations and iterations, and we were not good enough. And we kept on building and we kept on iterating and iterating and iterating. But we almost ran out of cash. And then we had this lucky day that Microsoft decided to invest, and so did Qualcomm. The funny part is that I had this dialogue with Qualcomm Ventures and they told me that they're not sure why is that important for them. And I read someplace that they did not invest at Twitter at $55 million. And this is exactly what I told them, "May I remind you that you did not invest in Twitter at $55 million valuation. This is where Waze is today." And obviously different story, but that was the fear of missing out, the FOMO was [inaudible 01:14:58]
turns.zh: 我们没有改变方向。2010年时，我们还不够成熟，仍在产品与市场匹配的反复迭代中。但我们几乎耗尽了资金。幸运的是，微软和高通在那时投资了我们。有趣的是，我和高通风投谈过，他们说不确定为什么这对他们很重要。我曾读到他们没有以5500万美元的估值投资Twitter。我当时就告诉他们：“提醒你们一下，当时你们没有以5500万美元的估值投资Twitter。而这就是Waze今天的处境。” 显然情况不同，但这就是错失良机的恐惧，FOMO（害怕错过）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I was going to say, good FOMO.
turns.zh: 是啊，我正想说，这才是好的FOMO。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: But the result was that we had enough cash to keep on trying and keep on iterating and iterating and iterating. And eventually we ended up to be very successful. So that was not about pivoting or changing directions or doing anything dramatic. We basically say, okay, we will need to reduce costs dramatically. We decided that we are not ... By the way, what we did is we reduced the salary of the management only. And to a certain extent I would say people didn't even know. We decided in the management meeting that this is what we're going to do. And if push come to shovel, then we will do the next step and the next step and the next step. But we were eventually able to raise capital. So in that sense, the nearly die was a matter of state of mind, but we did not run out of cash, we raised capital just before that.
turns.zh: 然而结果是，我们有足够的现金继续尝试，不断迭代、迭代、再迭代。最终我们取得了巨大成功。所以这并非是关于业务转型、方向调整或采取激烈行动的问题。我们基本上就是说，好吧，我们需要大幅削减成本。我们决定不……顺便说一下，我们只削减了管理层的薪资。在某种程度上，我觉得人们甚至都不知道这件事。我们在管理层会议上决定这么做。必要时，我们会采取下一步行动、再下一步、再下一步。但最终我们还是成功筹集到了资金。从这个角度看，濒临倒闭更多是心态问题，而非资金短缺——我们在资金告急前刚好筹到了资金。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The story is actually really illustrative of a point I was thinking as you were talking, which is that product market fit crisis often also leads to a cash crisis from investors not wanting to invest.
turns.zh: 这个故事其实很好地说明了你说话时我一直在思考的一个观点：产品与市场不匹配的危机往往也会导致投资者不愿投资而引发资金危机。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: In many cases, yes, in many cases.
turns.zh: 是的，很多情况下确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You get a double whammy.
turns.zh: 这简直是双重打击。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: But to a certain extent I would say no. Product market fit basically means that you go back to square one. The other alternative that you have, and by the way it's also valid, is if you are unable to convince your existing investors to reinvest in the company in order to build the new part of the journey, the new journey, then you know what? Shut down the company and restart a new company that is doing exactly that. And that's a bigger threat for investors because they are not part of the new journey. Now, they might want to say, "Oh, the company owns the IP." The know-how is the people, owned by the people, not the company.
turns.zh: 但在某种程度上，我认为并非如此。产品与市场不匹配基本上意味着你得从头再来。另一种可行的选择（同样可行）是，如果你无法说服现有投资者重新投资公司以开启新征程，那么你知道吗？那就关闭公司，重新创立一家专注于此的新公司。这对投资者来说是更大的威胁，因为他们无法参与新征程。如今，他们可能会说：“哦，公司拥有知识产权。”但关键技术在于人才——人才归人才所有，而非归公司所有。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you avoid the crisis? A lot this advice is here, you have a crisis, here's how to deal with it. Any advice for how to avoid falling into a crisis as a founder?
turns.zh: 如何避免危机？很多建议都聚焦于“危机已至，如何应对”。作为创始人，对于如何避免陷入危机，有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Number one answer is no. Don't worry, you will face crisis. And if you worry, you're still going to face crisis. Number two is that, look, it's way easier to deal with a crisis if you have plenty of cash in the bank. So if you can raise capital and maintain higher level of cash in the bank, it will help you to go through the next crisis, but it's not going to avoid it. So always be funded is a good advice. But in general, look, you do not prepare for the next crisis because you don't know what kind of crisis it's going to be next. And you can assume that there will be the next crisis. Trust me, there will be the next crisis. And then the most important part is that you analyze that fast and then you act fast. But you cannot prepare for it because you don't know where it's going to come from. And this is really, really important. The best preparation is that if you have plenty of cash. In general I would say if you have plenty of cash, then this is going to help you for many things.
turns.zh: 首要建议是：别担心。你注定会面临危机。若你担忧，危机仍会找上门。第二点是，如果你银行账户里有充足现金，应对危机会容易得多。所以若能成功融资并维持较高现金储备，将助你度过下一场危机，但无法完全避免。因此，保持资金充足是明智之举。但总体而言，你无法为下一场危机做准备，因为你无法预知它何时来袭。这点至关重要。最佳准备方式就是储备充足现金。总的来说，我认为充足现金将助你应对诸多挑战。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When you say plenty of cash, do you have any advice, kind of common advice of have 18 months of runway, is there anything there you'd recommend for founders?
turns.zh: 你提到的“充足现金”，有没有什么常见建议，比如“保持18个月的运营资金”之类的，能给创始人提些建议吗？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: And this is really depending on the CEOs and their risk attitude. Some of my CEOs prefer to have two to three years of run rate. They basically say, "This is my comfort zone. I know that I can restart if I need to. I know that I can suffer major crisis. I know that I can go into new direction if I want to. I know that I can expand and try something completely different if I want to." And this is not necessarily as a result of a crisis. So maybe you basically say here is an opportunity and I have the cash to do that. (01:19:22): My general rule will be around 18 month. Are you okay with 12 month? Yeah, if you risk taker, bigger risk taker then you can survive with 12 month. But the challenge is that, look, if you have shorter period of time, then you don't have enough time to execute, you need to focus on fundraising all the time. And you want to focus on creating value and not just bringing cash into the company.
turns.zh: 这实际上取决于CEO们及其风险偏好。我的有些CEO更倾向于有两到三年的运营周期。他们基本上会说：“这是我的舒适区。我知道如果需要的话，我可以重新开始。我知道我能承受重大危机。我知道如果愿意的话，我可以转向新方向。我知道如果想扩展并尝试完全不同的东西，我也可以做到。” 这并不一定是因为遭遇了危机。可能你只是觉得这里有机会，而我有现金可以投入。（01:19:22）我的通用规则是大约18个月。你能接受12个月吗？可以，如果你更愿意冒险，承担更大风险，那么12个月也行。但挑战在于，如果时间周期太短，你就没时间执行计划，只能一直专注于筹集资金。而你本应专注于创造价值，而不只是为公司引入资金。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Obviously the downside of raising more runway is you're giving away more of your company, but it's always this trade off, how much to sell, how money to get. Being a founder, what a tough gig. And I'm going to come back to this quote you had that I shared at the beginning of the podcast, which is building a startup is a journey from one crisis to the next.
turns.zh: 是的。显然，筹集更多资金的弊端是让出更多公司股份，但这始终是个权衡——出售多少股份，筹集多少资金。作为创始人，这份工作太难了。我要回过头谈谈你开场时提到的那句话：创业是一次从一个危机到下一个危机的旅程。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Yeah. It goes back into how ... the other three dimensions of a startup, it's a roller coaster journey with ups and downs and ups and downs, and it's a journey of failures because we are trying to build something new that no one did before so we tried multiple things. For that, Albert Einstein used to say that if you haven't failed that because you haven't tried new things before. And it's a long journey, it's a very long journey. In particular, the longest part is until you figure out product market fit. And now I add the fourth dimension of that, that this is a journey from one crisis to the next one.
turns.zh: 是的。这又回到了创业的其他三个维度——这是一次过山车般的旅程，起起落落，充满失败，因为我们试图创造前所未有的新事物，所以会尝试多种方法。正如阿尔伯特·爱因斯坦所说，如果你从未失败，那是因为你从未尝试过新事物。这是一段漫长的旅程，特别是找到产品与市场的契合点之前的阶段。现在我要加上第四个维度：这是一次从一个危机到下一个危机的旅程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How many companies have you started, 10 last time I saw?
turns.zh: 你创办过多少家公司？上次我看到是10家？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Yeah, about, a little bit more than that, yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，比那还要多一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A little bit more than that.
turns.zh: 多一点。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Not all of them are going to be successful, but most of them are.
turns.zh: 并非所有公司都能成功，但大多数都能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In some form. And you just keep doing it. You're a glutton for crisis is what I'm hearing here.
turns.zh: 以某种形式存在。你就一直做下去。这听起来你像是个危机爱好者。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: I'm not here for the crisis, I'm there for the value creation.
turns.zh: 我来这里不是为了危机，而是为了创造价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Uri, is there anything else that you wanted to share that you think might be helpful to get into before we wrap up?
turns.zh: 乌里，你还有什么想分享的吗？在结束前再聊聊。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: I really like this podcast, I really like it.
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢这个播客，真的很喜欢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Me too.
turns.zh: 我也是。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: And hopefully, in my mind, this is my mindset of a teacher, my destiny is about value creation, and if this podcast or this book, this one, can help people to become more successful, then I fulfill my destiny.
turns.zh: 希望在我看来，这就是我作为教师的心态，我的命运在于创造价值，如果这个播客或这本书能帮助人们变得更成功，那我就完成了我的使命。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Uri, I'm so delighted to be helping you fulfill your destiny. Two final questions. Where can folks find the book? When is it for sale? And then just how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 乌里，我很高兴能帮助你完成使命。最后两个问题。听众在哪里可以找到这本书？何时上市？然后听众如何能对你有所帮助？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: The book is going to be published in about a month from now. And it is already available for pre-orders on Amazon, but later on it will be on bookstores throughout the US and Canada and so forth.
turns.zh: 这本书大约一个月后就会出版。目前已在亚马逊上开放预售，之后会陆续登陆美国和加拿大各地的书店等平台。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's the date it'll be published because we're recording this ... Maybe it's coming out around the time we publish this. So what's the date?
turns.zh: 请问出版日期是哪天？因为我们正在录制这个节目……可能正好赶上我们发布这个节目的时间。那么具体日期是哪天呢？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: I think it's February 15th.
turns.zh: 我想是2月15日。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great. I think this is coming out right around there, so perfect timing.
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。看来出版时间正好合适，真是天时地利。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: So perfect timing. And you can follow me on LinkedIn or you can go to my website, urilevine.com. And I want you to read the book. End of the day, you asked me at the beginning what do I want to accomplish? Do I want people to buy the book or read the book? And I told you, "Look, everything that I'm trying to do in my life is about doing good and doing well." So buying the book is the doing well part of it and reading the book is the doing good part of it. And I want you to read the book.
turns.zh: 真是天时地利。大家可以关注我的领英账号，或者访问我的网站urilevine.com。我希望大家能读一读这本书。最初你问我想达到什么目标？是希望人们购买这本书，还是希望他们阅读这本书？我当时回答说，“看，我这辈子所做的一切都是为了行善、追求卓越。”所以购买这本书是追求卓越的部分，而阅读这本书则是行善的部分。我希望大家能读一读这本书。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so good. Uri, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 太好了。乌里，很感谢你今天能来。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Thank you, appreciate it.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，非常感激。
